title: Inside Mumbai and Pune's Ganpati Murti Workshops as Ganesh Chaturthi Draws Near
excerpt: From Parel's storied workshops to eco-friendly innovations shipping worldwide, murti-makers are preparing for the ten-day festival starting September 14.
body:
• As Ganesh Chaturthi approaches on September 14, murti workshops across Mumbai and Pune are in full swing, with artisans crafting thousands of idols ranging from small household murtis to towering 22-foot installations
  • Eco-friendly innovations are reshaping the craft, with paper-mache Ganpati idols weighing just 2.5 kg compared to 20 kg for traditional clay, and shipping to NRI communities worldwide
  • Mumbai's regulatory crackdown on Plaster of Paris idols has accelerated the shift toward sustainable materials, even as production costs rise

With Ganesh Chaturthi less than a month away, the sprawling murti workshops of Mumbai's Parel and Lalbaug neighbourhoods and Pune's artisan clusters are buzzing with activity. Sculptors, painters, and craftspeople are working around the clock to meet the surge in demand for Ganpati idols — continuing a tradition that has defined these workshop districts for generations.

From renowned studios like Siddhivinayak Arts and Peshwa Arts in Mumbai's Parel to artisan hubs in Solapur and Pune, workshops across Maharashtra are preparing murtis in sizes ranging from small home-worship idols to towering community installations reaching 22 feet, according to local artisan reports and workshop tour documentation.

A Living Craft Heritage

The art of murti-making in Mumbai is a family affair that often defies professional boundaries. According to a report by The Better India, idol-makers in the city include government designers with diplomas from the J.J. School of Arts, scriptwriters for advertising agencies, and engineers — all of whom return to their family workshops during the festival season.

https://x.com/timesofindia/status/2090038569729438086

Avinash Patkar, a designer at the central government's Regional Design and Technical Development Centre, spends his festival months sculpting idols alongside his family. His daughter Gautami, a commerce graduate, specialises in paper-mache work — a painstaking process that produces fewer idols but carries deep personal significance.

Reshma Khatu of the well-known Khatu Ganesh workshop took over idol-making operations after her father's death, working alongside her team from June to October. "Continuing my father's legacy was more important to me," she told The Better India.

The Eco-Friendly Revolution

Mumbai's regulatory crackdown on Plaster of Paris (PoP) idols has accelerated a shift toward environmentally sustainable materials. Artisans across the city are adopting natural clay, paper-mache, and even seed-embedded designs that can grow into plants after immersion.

One Mumbai artisan has spent over a decade crafting Ganpati idols from eco-paper — a mixture of calcium powder, processed paper pulp, and layered paper interiors. The results are striking: a standard two-foot paper Ganpati weighs just 2.5 to 3 kg, compared to 20 kg for a clay idol of the same size, according to a report by ANI.

"The biggest USP of our paper Ganpati is that it's a breeze to carry and absolutely eco-friendly."

— Mumbai-based eco-friendly idol artisan, via ANI

The Vaste family's Eco Shree Ganesha Arts, operating for over two decades, has pioneered a "Green Ganesha" made from red soil, organic fertiliser, natural colours, and hibiscus seeds. After immersion, the idol dissolves and sprouts into a flowering plant. Dattadri Kothur's "Tree Ganesha" concept takes a similar approach, embedding seeds that germinate when water is poured over the dissolved idol.

NRI Demand Drives Innovation

The lightweight, durable construction of eco-friendly idols has opened a growing international market. Shipments of paper-mache Ganpati idols are already reaching Indian diaspora communities in the United States, Canada, Dubai, Australia, and the United Kingdom, with most dispatched well in advance to meet shipping timelines.

"These idols are going international," one artisan told ANI. For NRI families, the appeal is clear — finding eco-friendly idols abroad remains a challenge, and the lightweight construction makes long-distance courier practical.

However, rising tariffs and shipping costs threaten this nascent export market. "Courier costs have already begun to worry our customers. If shipping becomes too expensive, we might see a drop in sales," the artisan said. Many of the 2026 international orders were dispatched before tariff increases took effect.

What's Next

Ganesh Chaturthi falls on September 14 this year, with the ten-day festival concluding with the grand visarjan processions. Mumbai's landmark pandals — including Lalbaugcha Raja and Chinchpokli Cha Chintamani — are preparing their own large-scale installations, drawing devotees and tourists alike.

For the artisans, the weeks ahead represent both the culmination of months of work and the continuation of a craft that bridges faith, art, and increasingly, environmental consciousness. Workshop tours on platforms like BookMyShow are also helping urban residents connect with the tradition, offering hands-on clay idol-making sessions in cities including Mumbai and Pune.
